title: The Mystery of the Fading Tonic
markdown:
The Willowkin of the Whisperwood were like walking saplings: rustling voices, eyes like dewdrops, green skin that usually shimmered with life. They caught sniffles. A chill might make their leaves droop. Nothing Commander Sol’s Glow-Moss Tonic could not usually chase off, like sunshine chasing fog. Brewed from the softest glowing moss in the deepest caves, it was not a charm. It was a medicine. A little bottle that had, for years, been enough.

One spring, as the first tender buds unfurled, the tonic lost its sparkle. Willowkin who drank it still coughed, leafy chests rattling. They still shivered, even when the sun was warm. Vibrant green faded toward sickly yellow-brown. The cheerful clinic, once filled with chirps and rustles of mending, began to hum with a low worried murmur. Commander Sol, steady as an ancient oak, looked more worried than anyone had seen her. Brow furrowed. Kind eyes shadowed.

Rafi arrived, a young drone pilot with eyes as bright as a new copper coin, and Thimble, a magpie with feathers like polished obsidian and a mind sharper than a jeweller’s needle. Thimble noticed small things other people missed: a lost button, a glint in the grass, and patterns. Rafi trusted her completely. They had a language of nudges, chirps, meaningful glances.

“Commander Sol,” Rafi said, concern clear in a room that already knew how to worry. “We’ve come to help. Thimble noticed something peculiar about the Willowkin who are still sick.”

Sol sighed, like leaves in a weary breeze. Her hands, usually sure as she prepared remedies, rested on her polished desk. “The Glow-Moss Tonic is not working as it should. They linger. As if the sickness has grown too stubborn for the moss.”

Thimble, perched on Rafi’s shoulder, chirped, bright black eyes on Sol. She had been watching the sick — and Sol’s work table, where the commander studied the wee beasties called bacteria.

Under the magnifying lens they were tiny wriggling specks. Thousands. When Sol added a single drop of tonic to a glass dish, most curled up, slowing, fading. A very few did not mind at all. They kept wiggling, strong and steady. Some even seemed faster, as if the tonic were a mild breeze.

Rafi frowned, stroking Thimble’s dark head. “So the tonic wasn’t stopping all of them. Only some.”

“Exactly.” A spark of hope cut the gloom. “Thimble noticing those few survivors — that is the important part.”

Sol guided them to a sun-dappled room at the back of the clinic. Rows of small clear dishes sat under soft warm lights. Miniature battlegrounds. She pointed to one, liquid alive with moving dots. “We’ve been adding the tonic to the Willowkin’s water for years, just to be on the safe side. A constant gentle bath for those bacteria.”

Thimble saw the pattern. In dishes treated for a long time, the survivors were the ones a little tougher from the start, with a knack for resisting. The weaker ones had perished. The stronger had a clear path. They had multiplied, become the majority. The microscope hummed. Sterile clinic smell. Thimble’s eyes darted across the wriggling world on the slide.

“When you expose a lot of microbes to something meant to stop them,” Sol said, quiet awe in her voice, “most die. That is its job. The very few that can survive — naturally a little resistant — get the field. They become the new majority. Selected, because their competition is gone.”

Rafi’s eyes widened. The well-intentioned constant use had not only treated the Willowkin. It had trained the bacteria. The tonic was no longer a surprise. A familiar opponent.

“So we can’t use it for every little sniffle. If we keep exposing all of them, even the weak ones, we help the strong get stronger. Soon, when someone is really sick, it will not work.”

Sol nodded. “Selection pressure. Use a medicine too often, or when it is not truly needed, and the resistant ones survive and multiply. Then the hero becomes weak.” She looked at the dishes. “Like always picking the fastest runners. Eventually only the fastest are left, and the race is no race.”

Thimble bobbed her head. “So what do we do?”

“Use it wisely. Reserve the Glow-Moss Tonic for the most serious illnesses, when their own defences cannot fight a fierce infection. For a common cough, a mild chill, let their bodies work. Give the tonic its best chance when it is needed most.”

They spent the next hours going dish by dish, marking which cultures still slowed when the moss touched them and which sailed on as if the drop were water. Rafi wrote the pattern in his notebook. Thimble hopped from rim to rim, never pecking the glass, only watching. Outside, the Whisperwood breathed. Inside, the clinic’s worry settled into something quieter: a plan.

Sol took the everyday bottles off the waiting-room tray that same afternoon. Mild sniffles would get rest, warm steam, and time. The Glow-Moss Tonic went to a high shelf, labelled for fierce infections only. A few Willowkin grumbled, wanting the familiar sparkle for a drooping leaf. Sol did not argue. She showed them a dish where the tonic now did almost nothing, and let the wriggling do the talking.

Rafi flew a short circuit over the Whisperwood at dusk, not hunting treasure but counting clinic lanterns. Fewer than last week. Thimble rode the drone’s rail in silence, a dark comma against the pale sky. The moss caves still glowed far below, patient as ever. The problem had never been the moss. It had been how often they asked it to work.

Later that week a young Willowkin named Pip stubbed a toe on a root and developed a nasty infection; leaves wilted alarmingly. Sol, brow clear, administered the tonic carefully. Colour returned. Leaves unfurled. Cheerful chatter filled the clinic. Rafi and Thimble watched, a quiet accomplishment between them.

It was not only flying drones, or shiny trinkets. It was keeping the remedies strong. Tiny creatures always adapting. Wisdom in how the gifts are used. Healing’s light, if they were careful, still shining.

They stood a moment in the doorway after Pip’s leaves had unfurled, the clinic’s murmur turning cheerful again. No one made a speech. Sol rinsed the dropper and set the bottle back on the high shelf, not the everyday tray. Thimble’s bright eyes caught the bottle’s glow and then looked away, as if even she understood some shinies were meant to be spent rarely.

Rafi felt it settle, solid as a well-tuned drone on a clear day, and wondered what else would need that same restraint — a light used less often, so it still worked when the dark was real.
characters: Rafi (a drone pilot), Thimble (a magpie), Sol (a commander)
